request: Rewrite this help text for someone who has never used a shared calendar. Keep it under 90 words. Return only the finished text. Facts: a private event is visible only to its creator; inviting someone reveals the title, time and location to that person; inviting someone does not reveal any other private events; a busy block shows coworkers that the time is unavailable without showing the event title. Draft: 'Our calendar empowers sophisticated privacy controls so you can unlock collaboration at your own pace. Private mode is a privacy-forward approach to event management. Inviting participants changes the visibility paradigm for invited participants. Busy blocks help facilitate availability awareness across your organization.'

Edit this personal essay opening to deepen its effect. Stay under 180 words. Preserve the narrator's slightly prickly humour and the supplied events; don't invent further biography or turn it into advice. Return only the revised opening. Draft: 'I kept the tin because it was a good tin. This is the defence I make, which would be convincing if the house did not contain eleven other good tins. My father used this one for screws. I use it for the buttons that come in little packets with new clothes, although I have never once replaced a button. The lid goes on crooked. You have to give it a small sideways shove. I am forty-three and still doing things the way he showed me, including things that do not work especially well. It is an interesting example of the way everyday objects can preserve important memories of people who are no longer here.'

Write a 220–300 word opinion piece for a neighbourhood newsletter arguing that our new public square needs some unprogrammed time. Take the opposing concern seriously. Use these facts and observations only; reasoning and proposals are welcome, invented statistics or incidents are not. The square has a small stage, six benches and movable chairs. The council's proposed calendar books an organised activity for every Saturday afternoon during its first three months. Supporters say a busy calendar will make the square feel welcoming and justify the money spent. Two nearby residents have said they would like somewhere to sit without buying anything. A square can be used without an event being scheduled. Give the piece a title. It should have an actual thought worth considering, not a campaign slogan or a list of amenities.

Tidy this note enough to send to a friend. Keep it recognisably mine, including some of the awkwardness. Don't turn it into a polished greeting-card message. Return only the note, no commentary. Draft: 'Hey. Thank you for coming over yesterday. I know I said I was fine and then talked for, I don't know, most of the afternoon. The soup was very good but mostly I was glad you were there. I have washed the container. This is apparently the practical thing I can report just now. Anyway. Thank you.'

Draft a 180–230 word speech for the opening of a volunteer-run repair café. It should sound good aloud, feel welcoming to someone embarrassed about bringing a broken object, and have one light moment that fits the occasion. Facts: volunteers can look at small electrical appliances, clothing and bicycles; there is no promise that an item can be fixed; visitors stay with their item and can learn alongside the volunteer; the café runs on the first Sunday of each month; work on mains-powered appliances is handled only by qualified volunteers. Do not invent a founding story, quotes, statistics, names or a repair success. Return only the speech.

Give three concise editorial notes on this short poem. Don't rewrite it. I want it to remain uncertain whether the speaker is waiting for a person, a season, or something else. Poem: 'I leave the gate / as you left it. / The hinge keeps / its small complaint. / By evening / the garden has moved / a little farther / into the path.'

Turn these notes into a 140–190 word review of a fictional exhibition called 'Ordinary Measures'. Have a point of view; stay within what the notes support. Don't add artist biography, audience reactions, artistic intentions or observations that aren't here. Notes: twelve photographs of kitchen tables, all shot from above; no people visible; three photographs include rulers beside ordinary items; one ruler lies beside a half-peeled orange, another beside a folded napkin; frames evenly spaced; final photograph shows an empty table with a pale rectangular mark where something once sat. My response: the exhibition became interesting when measuring stopped looking neutral. I found the repetition slow at first. I don't want the review to pretend that every choice worked.
